Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette:
Arjun is a 35-year-old South Asian man who works as a tax consultant in a mid-sized accounting firm in suburban New Jersey. He is married, the father of a toddler, and by most external measures has rebuilt a life of quiet stability since returning from a fourteen-month deployment with an international humanitarian relief organization in a conflict zone in the Middle East. He presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 52, referred by his primary care physician after his wife reported that he had become, in her words, "unreachable."

The events that most clearly organized his current symptom picture occurred during the final weeks of his deployment, when the field hospital where he worked as a logistics coordinator was struck by shelling. He was present when a section of the supply warehouse caught fire. In the chaos that followed, he could not locate two local staff members he had been responsible for evacuating. By the time the fire was suppressed, both had been killed. Arjun had been the one who drew up the shift schedule that placed them there. The smell of burning materials - acrid, oily smoke - filled the air for hours afterward, and he stood at the perimeter watching the site, unable to move, certain that something irreversible had happened because of a decision he had made. He attended both men's funerals in the days that followed, standing at the gravesides in a country not his own, feeling entirely outside of himself.

Since returning home, certain experiences carry that afternoon back into his body with a force that startles him. The smell of smoke - from a neighbor's fireplace, from a candle his wife lights in the evenings - stops him mid-movement, and when it does, his body appears to know before his mind does: his shoulders round forward, his head drops, and he finds himself in what feels like a physical echo of crouching beside rubble. The memories that surface in these moments are not linear; he cannot reconstruct the sequence of what happened with any clarity, and this disorganization itself becomes a source of distress, as though the fragmentation proves something damning about his character. When the smell of smoke reaches him, he will leave the room immediately, sometimes covering his face with his hands as he goes - a gesture that began as a practical response to the odor but has since become reflexive. He avoids the firm's annual holiday party, his wife's cousin's wedding last spring, and any occasion that might require him to feel something resembling hope or pleasure, because he has come to believe, with a quiet conviction that frightens him, that he no longer has the right to those feelings. This belief - that he failed to protect the people in his care - has become structurally load-bearing in his psychology. It shapes how he moves through the world: the avoidance of positive events is not merely emotional numbing but a form of self-imposed sentence.

The appraisals themselves feed back into his vigilance in a way that has made his nights nearly unworkable. He is certain that the world is not the ordered, predictable place he once believed it to be, and this shattered certainty means that ordinary sounds - a door closing in the hallway, his toddler knocking over a cup - produce a startle response that leaves him shaking. At night, he cannot feel safe; he lies awake listening to the house settle. His hypervigilant state keeps him in a condition of readiness that, paradoxically, makes the memories more accessible: the body already primed for threat finds it easier to slip into the sensory texture of that afternoon. When a colleague raises his voice in a meeting - not in anger, simply with emphasis - Arjun's concentration collapses entirely, the threat signal pulling him back toward the perimeter of the burning warehouse, and the shame that follows the memory makes him feel more isolated from his colleagues than before. His avoidance of the firm's client site visits, which began because one location is near a crematorium, has been noticed by his supervisor and attributed to disengagement. The more he withdraws, the more his sense of isolation solidifies into something that feels like evidence rather than symptom. He came to seek help not after a single crisis but after his wife found him sitting in the darkened kitchen at 3 a.m., face in his hands, and he could not explain to her - or to himself - what he was waiting for. What he most fears is that there is no explanation that does not confirm what he already believes: that he is, at his core, a man who failed when it mattered.
